outcome: Nothing in the window (after 26 January 2024) gives a closed form, a verified asymptotic or a new exact count for the number of n-step self-avoiding walks on the standard lattices; the nearest in-window event is a single-author 2025 preprint whose asymptotic-equivalence integral has no closed form, no error term and no proved step to the conjectured exponent, and the only AI-linked event (OpenAI's honeycomb-walk exponent family, October 2026) concerns exponents rather than counts and has Lean main theorems that are sorry-stubs.
problem_asks: (a) A function, indexed by walk length n, that models n-step self-avoiding walks: one function F(n), or a family F(n) over lattices, is asked for; the statement does not say whether F must be a formula, an algorithm, an asymptotic form or an approximation. (b) 'Model' is undefined in the statement: it could mean a count of the walks, an asymptotic for that count, a generating function, or a geometric parametrisation of a walk. (c) The objects are n-step self-avoiding walks; the statement names no lattice and no dimension, so its scope is open at the statement level. (d) No precision is required: the statement asks neither for an exact nor for an asymptotic output. It does not name the connective constant or any critical exponent. Context only, not part of the statement: the bullet's single link is to the Self-avoiding walk article, and its one reference is [35], Liskiewicz, Ogihara and Toda (2003) on the complexity of counting self-avoiding walks.

events.what_happened: Journal article 'On a function modeling an l-step self avoiding walk', AKCE International Journal of Graphs and Combinatorics 18(3), pp. 158-165 (2021), doi 10.1080/09728600.2021.1988831. Per the abstract text that a search engine returned (the publisher and DOAJ pages refused access), the paper introduces a 'needle function', a composition of compression-type maps R^n to R^n, and claims that it models an l-step self-avoiding walk for every natural number l, with the total length of the modelled walk bounded above and below by expressions in l, n and the compression parameters. The author name 'Theophilus Agama' came from a search-result summary and is not confirmed on any page I could read.
events.delivers: Claims a geometric parametrisation: a map from R^n to R^n whose image is said to model an l-step self-avoiding walk, with length bounds in l, n and the compression parameters. As far as the abstract text shows, 'models' is not defined by counting, asymptotics or enumeration. It is the closest literal match to the bullet's wording found in any source.
events.remains: Everything about counts: nothing in the visible text concerns the number of n-step self-avoiding walks, the connective constant or an asymptotic in n on any lattice. Whether the parametrised curves are self-avoiding lattice walks in the usual sense is not visible in the abstract text.
events.time_since_posted: about five years; no citing, reviewing or critical work found in search
events.directly_checkable: The needle function is given as an explicit composition of maps, so the modelling claim could be tested by hand once the full text is read. Not done: the full text was not reachable.
events.doubts: (1) The full text was not readable, so the definition of 'models', the proof and the length bounds are unchecked. (2) The 'compression' is a geometric contraction map (per the keywords and the search summary of a related arXiv family on compression and admissible points), not the polymer-physics compression, so the object may not be a lattice walk at all. (3) No citation, review, erratum or corrigendum was found in any search.
events.direction: Claims to answer the literal wording of the bullet, but in a geometric sense (a map that models a walk), not in the enumerative or asymptotic sense the bullet's linked article and reference point to. It is unclear whether it cuts toward or away from the problem as intended.
events.object: A composition of compression maps R^n to R^n (the 'needle function', written in the abstract as a composition over l of maps of the form Gamma_{a->i} o V_m), claimed to model an l-step self-avoiding walk. Explicit as a formula; not checked by me.
people: Theophilus Agama (name from a search-result summary; not confirmed on a page I could read)

events.what_happened: Maciej Liskiewicz, Mitsunori Ogihara and Seinosuke Toda, 'The complexity of counting self-avoiding walks in subgraphs of two-dimensional grids and hypercubes', Theoretical Computer Science 304(1-3), pp. 129-156 (2003), doi 10.1016/S0304-3975(03)00080-X; earlier versions at MFCS 2001 and ECCC report TR01-061 (2001). This is the bullet's own reference [35]. From the abstract as reproduced by a repository record (the page itself was not opened): counting self-avoiding walks of a fixed length in a subgraph of a two-dimensional grid is #P-complete, the full-grid question is only partly answered, and hypercube versions are complete for #EXP under exponential-time scaling. The two sources disagree on whom the question is attributed to (Valiant or Welsh).
events.revisions: ECCC TR01-061 (2001) and MFCS 2001 conference version precede the 2003 journal paper; the conference title is narrower ('...in Two-Dimensional Grid Graphs and in Hypercube Graphs').
events.delivers: A hardness result for the counting version of the question on subgraphs of two-dimensional grids: no efficient exact counting method is expected for that setting. It is not a formula for walk counts and does not give one for the full lattice.
events.remains: A formula or efficient algorithm for the number of n-step walks on the full square lattice and on the other standard lattices, which the abstract indicates is not settled by this paper; closed forms; asymptotic forms.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the 2003 journal version after refereeing

events.direction: Hardness of counting on a restricted setting. It bears on whether a formula or algorithm can be expected, and cuts against an easy counting function on those subgraphs; it does not decide the bullet's question.

events.what_happened: Irene Hueter, arXiv math/0108077, 'Proof of the Conjecture that the Planar Self-Avoiding Walk has Root Mean Square Displacement Exponent 3/4', first submitted 10 August 2001 and revised 17 August 2001 (v2). The abstract claims to prove Flory's (1949) conjecture that the square-lattice self-avoiding walk has root-mean-square displacement exponent nu = 3/4, using the point process of self-intersections of simple random walk and a 'weakly self-avoiding cone process'. The arXiv record shows no journal reference.
events.revisions: v1 10 Aug 2001; v2 17 Aug 2001 (a comment says the lower bound for the normalised first two moments of the weakly self-avoiding walk is not uniform as beta tends to infinity).
events.delivers: As claimed: the endpoint displacement of the square-lattice self-avoiding walk scales with exponent 3/4. This is one scaling exponent in d = 2. It gives no count of n-step walks and no function of n.
events.remains: The count c_n and its asymptotic form (the connective constant and the 11/32 exponent in the physics form); the scaling limit; every quantity other than the displacement exponent.
events.time_since_posted: about 25 years; I found no acceptance, erratum or verification in search
events.doubts: No journal reference is listed on arXiv. The two abstracts I read that address this area do not cite the claim as a proof: Lawler, Schramm and Werner (arXiv math/0204277, 2002) present the critical exponents as heuristic derivations from SLE conjectures, and Duminil-Copin and Hammond (arXiv 1205.0401, 2012) prove only sub-ballisticity in every dimension d at least 2. I did not read the full text of either, and this is not a verdict on Hueter's argument.
events.direction: Claims the conjectured value 3/4 for the square lattice, i.e. proves the conjecture for the displacement exponent. It cuts toward the physics prediction for that exponent, not toward a function for counts.

events.what_happened: Irene Hueter, arXiv math/0108120, 'Formula for the Mean Square Displacement Exponent of the Self-Avoiding Walk in 3, 4 and All Dimensions', first submitted 17 August 2001, 24 pages, no journal reference. The abstract, read through a summarising fetch and not quoted verbatim, claims a formula for the root-mean-square displacement exponent nu(d) on Z^d: nu(1) = 1 and nu(d) = max(1/4 + 1/d, 1/2) for d > 1. It says this settles conjectures dating to Flory (1949), gives values for d = 2 and d = 4 that match earlier expectations, and addresses d = 3, which the abstract says had no precise conjecture. It builds on the d = 2 paper (math/0108077).
events.revisions: v1 17 Aug 2001; no later version found.
events.delivers: As claimed: a closed formula for the displacement exponent nu(d) in every dimension. It is a function of the dimension d, not of the walk length n. It gives the scale of a walk, not a count or a model of the walk for each n.
events.remains: The counts c_n, their asymptotic form and the connective constant; any finite-n model; the d = 3 value is a new claim and I found no check of it.
events.time_since_posted: about 25 years; no acceptance, erratum or verification found
events.doubts: Same as the companion planar paper: no journal reference, and the two summaries of the field I read (Lawler, Schramm and Werner 2002; Duminil-Copin and Hammond 2012) do not refer to it as a proof in their abstracts. The d = 3 formula is a new claim with no check found.
events.direction: Claims a closed formula for the exponent in every dimension, consistent in the abstract with the d = 2 and d = 4 expectations; it cuts toward a formula for an exponent, not a function for walk counts.
events.object: The formula nu(1) = 1 and nu(d) = max(1/4 + 1/d, 1/2) for d > 1: an explicit function of the dimension d, claimed to be proved.

events.what_happened: Hugo Duminil-Copin and Stanislav Smirnov, arXiv:1007.0575, 'The connective constant of the honeycomb lattice equals sqrt(2+sqrt 2)', first submitted 4 July 2010; published in the Annals of Mathematics 175(3) (2012), pp. 1653-1665 (journal record seen in search, not opened). It proves the value that B. Nienhuis derived non-rigorously in 1982 for the hexagonal lattice, using a parafermionic observable for self-avoiding walks. A Lean evaluation page for the honeycomb constant also appeared in search (lean-lang.org), not opened.
events.revisions: v1 4 Jul 2010; later versions not read.
events.delivers: The exact exponential growth rate mu = sqrt(2+sqrt 2) of the number of n-step self-avoiding walks on the honeycomb lattice. Only the growth constant, for one lattice.
events.remains: The subexponential factor and exponent of the honeycomb counts; the function c_n for the honeycomb lattice; the connective constants of the square, triangular and cubic lattices, which remain numerical.

checked_by.who: Annals of Mathematics (refereed journal of record)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published after refereeing, vol. 175 no. 3 (2012); the journal listing was seen in search and not opened

events.direction: Confirms the predicted value of the growth constant for one lattice, cutting toward the physics prediction. It does not supply a function for the counts.

events.what_happened: Olivier Couronne (MODAL'X), arXiv:2211.16146, 'New upper bound for the connective constant for square-lattice self-avoiding walks', first submitted 29 November 2022. By modifying the automaton of Ponitz and Tittmann and considering loops up to length 26, the abstract gives 2.662343 as an upper bound for the connective constant of Z^2 (the search summary gives 2.662342426), improving the earlier 2.679192495. No journal reference is listed, and no computer or AI statement appears on the page.
events.delivers: An upper bound on the square-lattice connective constant of about 2.66234. It bounds the exponential growth rate of the counts on Z^2 only. It gives no function for the counts, no exponent and no lower bound.
events.remains: The exact value of the square-lattice connective constant (not known, per the Wikipedia article and the Erdos problem 528 page); the asymptotic form of the counts; any function for the counts.
events.time_since_posted: about 3 years 10 months; no acceptance or independent reproduction found
events.directly_checkable: The bound comes from a finite automaton computation that could in principle be rerun from the paper's description. Not done.
events.doubts: The bound is computer-generated from an automaton with loops up to length 26; the code and its output were not checked by me, and no independent reproduction was found. A search summary of a 2025 preprint (not opened) reported that it still cites the older 2.6792 figure; I did not verify this.
events.direction: Improves the upper bound on the exponential growth rate of the square-lattice counts. It moves a quantity the bullet's counts determine, but not the function or the exact value.

events.what_happened: Alexander Glazman, arXiv:1402.5376, 'Connective constant for a weighted self-avoiding walk on Z^2', first submitted 21 February 2014; Electronic Communications in Probability 20 (2015), paper 86. The walk lives on the dual Z^2 lattice; it may traverse a square twice but not cross an edge twice; a one-parameter family of critical weights, indexed by an angle theta in [pi/3, 2pi/3], is considered. At theta = pi/3 the model is the honeycomb walk, and the abstract says the author generalises the Duminil-Copin and Smirnov value sqrt(2+sqrt 2).
events.delivers: Per the abstract, an exact connective constant for a one-parameter family of weighted walks on the dual Z^2 lattice, with the honeycomb value as the endpoint theta = pi/3. The formula for general theta does not appear in the abstract text I read.
events.remains: The unweighted square-lattice walk the bullet names is not covered by this model. Counts for every theta; the function for the counts; the exponents.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published in volume 20 (2015), paper 86, after refereeing

events.direction: An exact connective constant for a weighted variant that contains the honeycomb case. It cuts toward exact values for weighted models only, not for the unweighted square-lattice walk.

events.what_happened: Youssef Lazar, arXiv:2504.13093, 'A lattice point counting approach for the study of the number of self-avoiding walks on Z^d' (primary math.PR; cross-listed math.CO, math.NT). Version 1 was submitted 17 April 2025 and version 2 on 20 April 2025; no version comments and no journal reference. The paper recasts the count of square-lattice self-avoiding walks as a count of integer points in multidimensional domains and applies Poisson summation. Theorem 1.1 states that c_n, the number of n-step walks, is asymptotically equivalent to an explicit multivariate integral I_n(0) (a sum over vectors in Z^{2n} of integrals of products of sinc functions and a Bessel J_1 term). Theorem 1.2 gives the same form for c_n(d), d >= 2. Section 5 treats the mean squared displacement of a typical walk in dimension 2. The paper gives no explicit error term, and it states the conjecture c_n ~ A n^{11/32} mu^n as a conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 17 Apr 2025 (15 KB); v2 20 Apr 2025 (15 KB), the current version; no version comments.
events.delivers: An asymptotic equivalence c_n ~ I_n(0) on Z^2 (and c_n(d) on Z^d, d >= 2), where I_n(0) is an explicit multivariate integral and not a closed form; no error term is given. Section 4.3 says that the author's 'hope' is that the truncated integral would follow the expected asymptotic; so the step to the conjectured form is not proved in the paper. It does not give the n^{11/32} mu^n form, the value of mu_c (the paper says only 2 < mu_c < 3), or the existence of lim c_{n+1}/c_n.
events.remains: (i) A closed form, or an evaluated asymptotic, for c_n. (ii) The exponent 11/32 and the constant A. (iii) The value of mu_c. (iv) The existence of lim c_{n+1}/c_n = mu_c, which the paper itself calls open. (v) Any error term. (vi) A computable function for c_n in the sense the bullet may intend.
events.time_since_posted: about 18 months (posted 17 April 2025); no citing or critical work found in search
events.directly_checkable: The integral I_n(0) can be evaluated for small n and compared with exact counts (exact counts are tabulated to around n = 79 in the transfer-matrix literature seen in search, not verified here). Not done.
events.doubts: (1) Theorem 1.1 is an asymptotic equivalence whose right-hand side is not evaluated, and the step to the closed exponent is explicitly left as a hope (section 4.3). (2) No error term is stated (section 2.3 says only that the main term is of interest). (3) Single author, no affiliation on the arXiv page, and no journal version after about 18 months. (4) I did not verify the proofs in sections 3 and 4; the full text was read only through a summarising fetch.
events.direction: Asserts an asymptotic formula for c_n in integral form, which would be a function modelling c_n in the asymptotic sense. It does not settle the enumerative formula, the exponent or the connective constant, and it cuts toward the bullet only if an integral asymptotic counts as 'a function to model'.
events.object: Not a counterexample. The candidate function is I_n(0): a Poisson-summation form of the lattice-point count, written as a sum over v in Z^{2n} of multivariate integrals of products of sinc and Bessel J_1 terms, claimed to be asymptotically equal to c_n as n grows. It is explicit but not closed, and it is not evaluated.

events.what_happened: Hacene Belbachir, Laszlo Major, Laszlo Nemeth and Laszlo Szalay, 'Step-constrained self-avoiding walks on finite grids', Journal of Combinatorial Theory Series A 218 (2026), article 106104, doi 10.1016/j.jcta.2025.106104. The open-access repository copy was blocked to me, so the description below comes from a search summary of the abstract. It counts self-avoiding walks of a prescribed length between diagonally opposite corners of a finite rectangular grid under step constraints; for two dimensions with three step directions it gives a closed-form expression, and a separate algorithm computes the counts faster; for higher-dimensional rectangular grids it gives a formula for walks exactly two steps longer than the shortest. The same group's 2024 Aequationes paper (Major, Nemeth, Pahikkala, Szalay) on walks with specified numbers of wrong steps is related and was not dated by me.
events.revisions: No arXiv preprint found. The date is from the DOI prefix (j.jcta.2025), not from an online date I could read.
events.delivers: For a restricted model (three step directions in two dimensions, finite rectangular grids, corner to corner), an explicit closed-form count of self-avoiding walks of a given length; for higher dimensions, a formula for walks two steps longer than minimal on finite rectangular grids. Restricted in each case to the stated grid and step constraints.
events.remains: The counts of self-avoiding walks on the infinite standard lattices (all step directions, Z^2 and Z^d); asymptotic forms; any function for c_n in the bullet's sense.

checked_by.who: Journal of Combinatorial Theory Series A (refereed journal)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published in volume 218 (2026), per the repository record; the paper itself was not read

events.time_since_posted: about one year since the 2025 DOI year
events.doubts: The paper was not read; the formulas and the AI status of the paper are unchecked beyond the repository record and the abstract summary.
events.direction: An explicit formula for a restricted-step, finite-grid analogue. It cuts toward closed forms for restricted models; it does not address the counts on the standard lattices.

events.what_happened: Sun Woo P. Kim and Gabriele Pinna, arXiv:2509.04568, 'Existence and bounds of growth constants for restricted walks, surfaces, and generalisations', submitted 4 September 2025 (one version). It introduces self-osculating walks, supersets of self-avoiding walks in which edges may touch at vertices but may not cross; it gives upper bounds for their connective constants on the square and triangular lattices, defines self-osculating surfaces and k-manifolds, proves that their growth constants exist with explicit bounds, and improves the upper bound for self-avoiding surfaces on Z^3. Read through a summarising fetch.
events.delivers: Upper bounds on the growth constants of self-osculating walks (a superset of self-avoiding walks) on the square and triangular lattices, and existence and bounds for surface growth constants. Not the connective constant of self-avoiding walks on Z^d.
events.remains: The self-avoiding walk connective constants and any counting function for them.
events.direction: Bounds for a neighbouring superset model. It moves a growth constant of a different model, not the self-avoiding walk one.

events.what_happened: Qidong He, arXiv:2508.01993, 'Upper bounds for the connective constant of weighted self-avoiding walks', versions 4 Aug, 11 Aug and 17 Aug 2025; Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical 58(50) (2025), article 505003. The method builds on Alm's upper-bound method and gives bounds as dominant eigenvalues of matrices; it is implemented in publicly available software (not named on the page). Version 3 says that relaxing Condition I extends the method to the full class of lattices Alm considered.
events.revisions: v1 4 Aug 2025; v2 11 Aug 2025; v3 17 Aug 2025 (current).
events.delivers: Numerical upper bounds on the connective constant of weighted self-avoiding walks, for Alm's class of lattices (per v3). Restricted to weighted walks.
events.remains: The unweighted self-avoiding walk connective constants and counts; exact values; any function for the counts.

checked_by.who: Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical (refereed journal)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published as 58(50), 2025, article 505003 (journal reference on the arXiv page)

events.direction: Upper bounds on the growth constant of a weighted variant, a different quantity from the unweighted walk count. It cuts toward numerical bounds for weighted models only.

events.what_happened: Benjamin Grant and Zhongyang Li, arXiv:2601.12571, 'Self-avoiding walks on cubic graphs and local transformations', version 1 on 18 January 2026 and version 2 on 16 February 2026; no journal reference. The paper proves a substitution principle: each degree-3 vertex of an infinite connected quasi-transitive cubic graph is replaced by a fixed three-port gadget, and the connective constant of the new graph is determined by a series for the gadget. It extends a Fisher-triangle relation of Grimmett and Li, treats bipartite graphs, shows that gamma and eta (and nu under a regularity hypothesis) are unchanged, and gives explicit gadget families whose connective constants are roots of algebraic equations.
events.delivers: Connective constants and unchanged critical exponents for self-avoiding walks on a class of cubic graphs obtained by gadget substitution, with explicit algebraic values for some gadgets. Restricted to that graph class, not Z^d.
events.remains: The counts and any function for them on Z^2 and Z^d.
events.direction: Exact connective constants for an explicit family of graphs that are not the standard lattices. It cuts toward exact values for that class only.

events.what_happened: Hemant Mishra, Shubham Singh, Rajeev Singh and Amit Raj Singh, arXiv:2512.24648, 'Quantum Computing Inspired Approach for Self-Avoiding Walk (SAWs): 2D lattice and 3D lattice SAWs for single chain enumeration'; version 1 on 31 December 2025, version 2 on 2 January 2026; 13 pages; no journal reference. The paper proposes a quantum-amplitude-estimation-based enumeration; per the abstract summary it reports enumerating square-lattice walks up to N = 71 in 26.9 minutes and cubic-lattice walks up to N = 40 in 13.06 minutes, presented as large speedups over earlier classical results. The square-lattice range coincides with the exact-enumeration range already known (Jensen 2004, as seen in search), so no new counts are claimed in the summary.
events.delivers: A claimed faster way to compute the counts already known up to N = 71 on the square lattice and N = 40 on the cubic lattice. No formula or function for the counts.
events.remains: A function or formula for c_n; any count beyond the known range.
events.directly_checkable: The square-lattice terms up to N = 71 can be compared with the known exact counts (OEIS A001411, as cited in search). Not done.
events.doubts: The speedup claims are not checked; the abstract summary does not show how the quantum routine's output was verified classically or how its resource cost was counted; the authors' affiliations are not shown on the arXiv page; no journal version.
events.direction: A claim about computation time for the counts, not a function for them. It bears on the algorithmic reading of the bullet only.

events.what_happened: Dmitrii Krachun and Christoforos Panagiotis, 'Quantitative sub-ballisticity of self-avoiding walk on the hexagonal lattice', Annals of Probability 54(3) (May 2026), pp. 1109-1125; the journal record quoted in search gives an early online date of 20 April 2026. It shows that with high probability a self-avoiding walk of length n stays within a ball of radius O(n/log n) on the hexagonal lattice, improving the o(n) bound of Duminil-Copin and Hammond (2012). It uses the Duminil-Copin and Smirnov parafermionic observable and a polynomial decay of bridge partition functions at criticality. The result was presented in talks from 17 December 2023 (Athens) onward; I did not find an arXiv posting, so the first written argument is not dated here.
events.revisions: No arXiv version found; the journal record is the only dated written version I could see.
events.delivers: A quantitative bound on the displacement of a hexagonal-lattice self-avoiding walk, O(n/log n) with high probability. Restricted to one lattice and to the displacement scale, not a count.
events.remains: The counts and any function for c_n on the hexagonal lattice; the exponent nu is not claimed by the bound as summarised.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published in vol. 54 no. 3, May 2026, per the journal record seen in search

events.time_since_posted: published May 2026; first written argument not located
events.direction: A displacement bound on a hexagonal walk, in the direction of the known scaling. It does not change the count.

events.what_happened: OpenAI, github.com/openai/math, a collection of mathematical manuscripts released on about 6 October 2026 (a secondary report gives 6 October; the repository's history file has an entry dated 7 October that concerns other families). Result family 237 is titled in the repository's Lean scope page 'The three-quarter exponent for honeycomb self-avoiding walk'; a secondary catalogue titles it 'The three-quarter diameter exponent for honeycomb walks' and counts 13 manuscripts. The scope page names four accompanying papers, whose folder names carry the date 26 September 2026: 'Polynomial vacuum representations and bridge mass for honeycomb walks'; 'Renewal and changes of law for critical honeycomb walks'; 'Critical strip-crossing mass on the honeycomb lattice'; 'Critical honeycomb chords with prescribed boundary endpoints'. The catalogue index also lists under family 237 'Mass and covering exponents for fixed-length honeycomb walks', 'Cylinder amplitudes and logarithmic bridge-length windows on the honeycomb lattice', 'Signed cylinder propagation and marked polygons on the honeycomb lattice', and two earlier untitled entries ('Uniform marked-polygon estimates and sharp finite bridge moments'; 'Cap-selected amplitudes and triangle chords for honeycomb walks'). The PDFs are stored as binary and I could not read their text. The scope page says the linked Lean formalization covers: finiteness of critical bridge measures; existence of the infinite-length free energy for the critical honeycomb self-avoiding walk partition function; strip-crossing weight comparable to N^(-1/4) and a return-path displacement moment comparable to N^(3/4); and bridge mass of order (1+h)^(-1/4). It states as outside its scope the h^(4/3+o(1)) mean-length law, the central-visit and hexagonal-chord exponents, the small-force exponent, the near-critical correlation scale, and the 3/4 spatial and moment laws.
events.revisions: Manuscripts dated 26 Sep 2026 (folder names and README header). The first public appearance I could establish is the repository release of about 6 October 2026. No revision of family 237 found; the repository history entry of 7 October 2026 concerns other families (three withdrawals and fourteen repairs).
events.delivers: Per the scope page and the family title, for honeycomb walks: (a) strip-crossing weights comparable to N^(-1/4) and return-path displacement moments comparable to N^(3/4), with constants uniform in N; (b) existence of the infinite-length free energy of the critical honeycomb self-avoiding walk partition function with force parameter; (c) finiteness of critical bridge sums. These are scaling and exponent statements for honeycomb walks, not a count c_n and not a function of n that counts walks. The 3/4 exponent is the value conjectured for two-dimensional self-avoiding walks. I could not read the manuscripts, so I cannot confirm what they prove beyond the scope page.
events.remains: The count c_n of n-step honeycomb walks and any function modelling it; the connective constant of the honeycomb lattice (already known from the 2010 result); the square lattice. By the scope page's own account, the h^(4/3+o(1)) mean-length law, the central-visit and hexagonal-chord exponents, the small-force exponent, the near-critical scale and the 3/4 spatial and moment laws are not covered by the Lean files; their status in the manuscripts is not verified by me.
events.time_since_posted: under a week at the time of this record

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 comparator files in the openai/math repository (lean/ComparatorChallenges)

events.directly_checkable: The four Lean files can be built with the repository's Lean toolchain; the main theorems and their sorry lines can be inspected directly. The manuscripts' statements can be checked by reading the PDFs, which I did not do.
events.doubts: (1) The Lean files do not prove the family's main statements. In each of four comparator files the main theorem's proof is 'sorry': HoneycombBridgeMassSupport.lean (finiteBridgeMassEstimate, sorry at line 73, docstring 'Trusted reference hole only; missing necessary main obligation.'); HoneycombBridgeFiniteness.lean (finite_bridge_sums, sorry at line 62); HoneycombFreeEnergy.lean (logPartition_tendsto, sorry at line 67); CriticalStripMass.lean (critical_strip_mass, sorry at line 75). The line numbers come from a summarising fetch and should be rechecked in the repository. The scope page says the formalization 'establishes' these results and states 'no sorry or axiom notes', which the files contradict. (2) The README says 'Some of the unformalized results could have issues' and that results are 'at different stages of verification'. (3) No named human author, referee or per-manuscript verification statement appears for this family. (4) The repository's title and manuscript count for the family (four papers on the scope page; 13 manuscripts in the secondary catalogue) do not agree. (5) Three other manuscripts in the collection were withdrawn after a sign error (not this family), so the collection has had errors. (6) The 3/4 exponent is a conjecture in the literature; the only earlier claimed proof I found is Hueter (2001), which has no acceptance on record.
events.direction: Claims scaling exponents and bounds for honeycomb self-avoiding walks: the 3/4 displacement law and the N^(-1/4) strip weight, and existence of the forced free energy. These are consistent with the conjectured 3/4 exponent and say nothing about the number of walks of each length. The direction cuts toward the exponent reading of the bullet, not the enumerative reading.

systems.name: an unreleased internal OpenAI model
systems.what_it_did: The README says the repository contains manuscripts and proof artifacts 'produced by an internal OpenAI model', and that the vast majority of results were obtained with one procedure using that model. The only exceptions it lists are work on the Riemann zeta zero-free region and the Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties; family 237 is not among them. The README says the model was posed about 4,000 problems. The README gives no per-family account of how the honeycomb manuscripts were produced beyond this general statement.

ai.disclosed_cost: On average, each result used three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute with that model (README). The model was posed approximately 4,000 problems (README).

summary: I ran 46 web searches and opened about 40 pages, including the bullet's Wikipedia entry (its only link is to the Self-avoiding walk article, and its one reference is [35], Liskiewicz, Ogihara and Toda 2003, on the complexity of counting walks), the Wikipedia Self-avoiding walk article (its unsolved-problem box asks whether a formula or algorithm can count such walks on any lattice, and it still lists the 11/32 law as a conjecture), and the Erdos problem 528 page (listed open, with no comments claiming progress and no entry in Tao's AI-contributions wiki). No in-window event gives a closed form, a verified asymptotic or a new exact count for the standard lattices. The close call is Lazar's April 2025 preprint, the only in-window event that supplies an asymptotic-equivalence function for square-lattice counts: Theorem 1.1 asserts c_n ~ I_n(0) with I_n(0) an explicit multivariate integral, not a closed form, with no error term, and section 4.3 says the step to the expected form is a hope rather than a proof. Whether that is 'a function to model n-step walks' depends on whether an unevaluated integral asymptotic qualifies; the bullet does not say. Other in-window events are neighbouring: Belbachir et al. (JCTA 2026) give closed-form counts for a restricted three-direction model on finite grids (not read directly; blocked); Kim and Pinna, He, and Grant and Li give bounds or exact values for weighted, self-osculating or cubic-graph models; Mishra et al. claim a quantum speedup for counts already known to n = 71; Krachun and Panagiotis quantify sub-ballisticity on the hexagonal lattice (the first written argument could not be dated). The AI search found one AI-linked event: OpenAI's repository (released about 6 October 2026), whose family 237 is a set of honeycomb-walk manuscripts on exponents and bridge masses, credited in the README to 'an unreleased internal OpenAI model' under one procedure with no named human authors. That family is not a counting result, and its four Lean scope files each prove the main theorem by sorry, which contradicts the scope page's claim of 'no sorry'. I could not read the manuscripts (the PDFs are stored as binary). Before 2024 there are two claims that match the bullet's wording more closely than anything else: Agama's 2021 'needle function' (a geometric map claimed to model an l-step walk; the full text was blocked, so this rests on an abstract snippet) and Hueter's 2001 papers claiming the planar 3/4 exponent and a dimension formula nu(d) = max(1/4 + 1/d, 1/2). I found no acceptance or refutation of either. The exact honeycomb connective constant (Duminil-Copin and Smirnov, 2010, Annals 2012) and its weighted extension by Glazman (2014, ECP 2015) are the only exact growth constants I found in refereed venues, and both are for models other than the square-lattice walk. Searches for AI involvement in square-lattice counts, the connective constant, Erdos 528, Epoch's open-problem list, AlphaEvolve and AlphaProof, and OpenAI's Astra release found no walk or lattice-path result.
competing_reading: Read the bullet as asking for an asymptotic function for c_n: then Lazar's Theorem 1.1 is the in-window event that supplies one, and the problem is partly addressed in a weak sense, though with no error term and an unproved step to the conjectured form. Read it as asking for an explicit or closed formula: then nothing in the window qualifies, and Belbachir et al. shows the restricted analogue only. Read 'model' geometrically, as the 2021 Agama paper does: then that paper is a claimed answer that predates the window and has no engagement on record. Read the OpenAI family as relevant because it treats the same walk, with honeycomb exponents as the closest the bullet gets to a 'function' for walk scale: then it is the only AI-linked event in scope, and its AI involvement is load-bearing by the lab's own account. Read it as out of scope because it neither counts nor models walks of length n and its Lean main theorems are unproven placeholders: then the only AI-linked event is outside the question, and the record shows no AI involvement in any counting result.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A referee report, or an independent numerical test, of Lazar's Theorem 1.1: evaluate I_n(0) for small n and compare it with exact counts, and check the approximation step in section 3.1. (2) The full text of Agama 2021, to see whether 'models' means a count, an asymptotic or a geometric parametrisation, and whether the length bounds are about the walk in the usual sense. (3) The OpenAI family 237 PDFs, read for their main theorems and for any statement about c_n; and a build of the four comparator files to see whether any main theorem is proved without sorry. (4) zbMATH or MathSciNet records for Hueter's two preprints, and any erratum or review. (5) The intent of the bullet's editors, which the Wikipedia article history or talk page might show: the bullet's only reference is the 2003 counting-complexity paper, which points toward a counting reading.

incomplete: (1) Agama 2021 was not read beyond a search snippet and a search summary (the publisher and DOAJ pages returned 403), so its definition of 'models', its length bounds and its author attribution are unverified. (2) The OpenAI family-237 manuscripts (four on the scope page, thirteen in the secondary catalogue) could not be read, so what they prove and whether any of them concerns walk counts is unverified; the Lean sorry findings and their line numbers come from a summarising fetch and should be rechecked in the repository. The per-family AI statement is the README's general statement, not a manuscript-level account. (3) The openai/math family index was read in seven summarised chunks rather than verbatim; no other family about self-avoiding walks was found, but the keyword scan was not a verbatim read. (4) Lazar 2025 was read through a summarising fetch of the HTML version; the proofs in sections 3 and 4 were not checked, and no citing or critical work was found by search (no Google Scholar or Scopus access). (5) Belbachir et al. 2026 was not read (blocked); its date is taken from its DOI year. (6) Krachun and Panagiotis have no arXiv version found, so the date of the first written argument is not established. (7) Couronne 2022, Glazman 2014 and Duminil-Copin and Smirnov 2010 were checked through abstracts only; the full texts were not read, and the journal records for the last two came from search snippets. (8) zbMATH and MathSciNet records were not reached for any pre-window claim. (9) Epoch's open-problems list and the full OpenAI Astra release were not read in full.
